title: 🏛️ From governance and business models to working technical systems

paras: How public needs, government policy, public/private organizations, procurement, employees, standards, networks, software and operations fit together.
Historical path: trade and social demand → government and institutions → industrial production → telegraph, radio and telecommunications → computing → internet → cloud and AI.

Implementation path: public or customer need → policy and budget → tender / contract → vendor selection → architecture and standards → manufacturing / procurement → deployment → service delivery → monitoring, maintenance and renewal.
These are explanatory paths, not rigid sequences: law, markets, technology and operations affect one another through feedback loops.

blocks.h2: Public, private, hybrid and regulated enterprises
paras: Government departments, statutory bodies and state-owned enterprises; distinguish public authority, public funding and public ownership.
Private companies, vendors, operators, service providers and customers; business decisions shaped by contracts and applicable regulation.
Public-private partnerships, joint ventures, concessions, outsourcing and mixed ownership; identify the actual allocation of risk, ownership and responsibility.
Publicly accessible services are not necessarily government-owned. A public internet service, public company and public-sector agency are different concepts.
Compare functions and boundaries without asserting literal equivalence.

blocks.h2: From authority to a service used by people
paras: Role: law, public policy, authorization, oversight and enforcement. Connection: regulations and permits constrain providers; funding and procurement may originate with public agencies.
Role: requirements, RFP/tender, evaluation, contract, acceptance. Connection: contractual obligations pass to selected providers and subcontractors.
Role: management, financing, delivery, hiring, supplier coordination. Connection: converts commercial obligations into engineering requirements.
Role: standards, chips, devices, cables, network design, software and integration. Connection: physical and digital components become a deployed system.
Role: Linux, routing, cloud, SRE, NOC, SOC, support and maintenance. Connection: monitored services deliver agreed outcomes and generate operational feedback.
Role: consume services, report incidents, measure usefulness. Connection: needs, payments, outcomes and feedback influence future policy and design.

Arrow meaning: ① → ② = policy/funding constraints; ② → ③ = commercial authorization; ③ → ④ = requirements/resources; ④ → ⑤ = deployment/handover; ⑤ → ⑥ = service delivery; ⑥ → ①/②/③ = feedback, accountability and demand. These are distinct from packet-routing arrows.
Business process: tender → vendor bid → evaluation → negotiation → contract → purchase order → delivery → inspection → invoice → settlement → renewal or escalation.

Technical analogies: discovery → request/response → validation → capability negotiation → interface contract → authorized invocation → payload transfer → acknowledgement → metering → versioning and error handling.

Actual standards to study: EDI and procurement documents; payment messaging; SLAs; HTTP APIs, OpenAPI, TLS, TCP/IP, BGP and DNS. A business procedure is not the same kind of protocol as a network wire protocol.

blocks.h2: Public connectivity project: from tender to Linux packet
paras: A government agency funds connectivity for schools. A tender defines coverage, security, equipment, uptime and reporting. A contracted operator sources routers, radio equipment or fiber, configures WAN connectivity, creates school LANs and VLANs, assigns IP addresses, secures traffic, and operates monitoring and incident response. A student's application request then travels through the local NIC, switch/AP, gateway, provider network and destination service.

India: examine the relevant ministry, DoT/WPC, TRAI, applicable procurement rules, operators and state/local agencies depending on project scope. U.S.: examine the applicable federal/state authorities, FCC where relevant, public procurement entities and operators. Regulatory responsibilities vary by service and jurisdiction.
Business-to-technical chain: funding → SLA → network design → AS/BGP or upstream transit → subnet/VLAN → NIC/driver → IP/TCP/TLS → API/service → monitoring and billing.

paras: B001–B003: trade, history, communications, governance, standards and supply chains. B004: regulation, organizational power and employees. rows: Independent policy domain; real AS means an internet routing-policy domain and may span or exclude corporate boundaries.
Multiple separately administered systems; political jurisdiction is not a routing domain.
Logical separation and permissions; departments can span many networks.
Operational grouping or geographic placement; not necessarily Layer 2 segmentation.
People have roles and authority; machines carry traffic and execute programs.
Policy-setting versus operational execution; neither directly maps to a router control plane.
Agreed responsibilities, interfaces and measurable commitments; legal contracts are not transport protocols.
Interorganizational dependency; business partnerships are not necessarily BGP peering.
Request, bid, approval, delivery and acceptance as a stateful process.
Evidence, accountability and controls; compliance also includes legal and human obligations.
